title: Formulas and Calculations
sequence: estimates, baselines and reserves are calculated in planning; variances, indices and forecasts in monitoring and controlling. Reuse the same formulas at every status date.

header.html: Process domain (41%) · the numbers behind Task 6 Plan and manage finance (quantify risk and contingency allocations, track spending, manage reserves), Task 8 Plan and manage schedule (estimate, analyze variation) and Task 9 Evaluate project status (measure, analyze and update metrics). Calculation questions are a minority of the exam (most items are scenario judgment), but they are quick points when the formulas are automatic.

[Beyond PMBOK 8] = exam-relevant, but PMBOK 8 does not print the formula (it may name the concept). PMBOK 8 prints the earned value table, the CPM day-1 formulas, TCPI, the triangular average and an EMV decision tree; the rest is standard exam practice.

html:
1How to Approach Calculation Questions

  1. Find what is asked (a value, a decision, or an interpretation) and the assumption words in the stem: "current performance will continue," "the variance was a one-time event," "the original plan is no longer valid," "both cost and schedule performance affect the remainder."
  2. List the given data with units; spot distractors (extra numbers).
  3. Write the formula, then compute. Keep fractions until the end and round once.
  4. Sanity-check the direction: CPI below 1 means EAC above BAC; TCPI above 1 means the remaining work must be done more efficiently; negative float means a constraint is violated.
  5. Check the convention (for example, CPM start on day 1 uses EF = ES + D − 1) and the sign (variances: actual minus plan is the wrong way round; PMBOK 8 uses EV minus the comparison value).
  6. If the numbers do not give a unique answer, choose the option that follows the stated assumption.

2Schedule Calculations (Process Task 8)

2.1 Duration from effort and quantity

Formula Use
Duration = effort ÷ (resources × availability) Beyond PMBOK 8 120 person-hours with 2 people each 75% available: 120 ÷ (2 × 0.75) = 80 elapsed hours
Parametric: quantity × hours per unit (PMBOK 8 examples: drawings × hours per drawing; meters of cable × hours per meter) 40 drawings × 12 hours = 480 hours
Analogous: the actual of a similar earlier activity or project, adjusted for known differences Quick, less accurate

2.2 Three-point estimates

Estimate Formula Example (O = 6, M = 9, P = 18)
Triangular (PMBOK 8) (O + M + P) ÷ 3 (6 + 9 + 18) ÷ 3 = 11
PERT / beta Beyond PMBOK 8 (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6 (6 + 36 + 18) ÷ 6 = 10
Standard deviation Beyond PMBOK 8 (P − O) ÷ 6 (18 − 6) ÷ 6 = 2 (variance 4)
Path or project Beyond PMBOK 8 Sum the expected durations on the critical path; SD = √(sum of variances) Variances 4, 9 and 2.25: total 15.25, SD ≈ 3.9

Probability bands [Beyond PMBOK 8]: ±1 SD ≈ 68.27%, ±2 SD ≈ 95.45%, ±3 SD ≈ 99.73%.

Probability of finishing by a date [Beyond PMBOK 8]: z = (deadline − expected duration) ÷ standard deviation. A larger z means a higher chance (z = 0 is 50%, z = 1 about 84%, z = 1.5 about 93%, z = 2 about 98%). A path with a lower mean but a large standard deviation can be riskier than the longest path: with a 42-day deadline, path A (mean 36, SD 4) has z = 1.5, about 93%, while path B (mean 34, SD 10) has z = 0.8, about 79%, so B is the riskier path although its mean is lower.

2.3 Critical path method (PMBOK 8 convention: the project starts on day 1)

Step Formula
Forward pass ES = the latest EF of the predecessors + 1; EF = ES + Duration − 1
Backward pass LF = the earliest LS of the successors − 1; LS = LF − Duration + 1
Total float LS − ES = LF − EF (zero on the critical path; negative = constraint violated)
Free float ES(successor) − EF(this) − 1 under the day-1 convention (older convention: ES − EF)
Critical path The longest path; it sets the shortest possible project duration

Worked example. A (3 days) is followed by B (4 days) and C (6 days) in parallel, and both precede D (2 days).

Activity Duration ES EF LS LF Total float
A 3 1 3 1 3 0
B 4 4 7 6 9 2
C 6 4 9 4 9 0
D 2 10 11 10 11 0

The critical path is A–C–D = 11 days. B's total float is 2 and its free float is 10 − 7 − 1 = 2. (PMBOK 8's own example: A = 5, B = 5, C = 10, D = 15 gives A–C–D = 30 days and B has 5 days of float.)

2.4 Compression, leads and lags

  • Crashing [Beyond PMBOK 8 formula]: extra cost per day saved = (crash cost − normal cost) ÷ (normal duration − crash duration). Crash only critical-path activities, cheapest per day first, and re-check the critical path after each step.
Activity Normal Crash Days saved Extra cost per day
A 10 days, 20,000 8 days, 23,000 2 1,500
B 6 days, 12,000 4 days, 14,000 2 1,000
C 8 days, 16,000 7 days, 18,000 1 2,000

If all three are critical and the project must shorten by 2 days: crash B twice for 2,000. For 3 days: B twice plus A once = 2,000 + 1,500 = 3,500.

  • Fast tracking: overlap activities normally done in sequence (no cost formula; adds risk and rework).
  • Lead subtracts time from the relationship (a successor can start earlier); lag adds waiting time. Durations never include them.

2.5 Schedule performance

SV = EV − PV; SPI = EV ÷ PV (Table 5-1: positive SV or SPI above 1 means ahead of schedule). Check the critical path before reacting: a low SPI on non-critical work may not threaten the end date (Topic 16).

3Cost and Earned Value (Process Tasks 6 and 9)

3.1 PMBOK 8 Table 5-1

Measure Formula Interpretation
Planned value (PV) Authorized budget for the work scheduled to date
Earned value (EV) Budget authorized for the work actually performed
Actual cost (AC) Cost actually incurred for the work performed
Budget at completion (BAC) Sum of all budgets for the work (the cost baseline)
Cost variance (CV) EV − AC Positive = under budget; negative = over
Schedule variance (SV) EV − PV Positive = ahead; negative = behind
Cost performance index (CPI) EV ÷ AC Above 1 under cost; 1 on cost; below 1 over cost
Schedule performance index (SPI) EV ÷ PV Above 1 ahead; 1 on schedule; below 1 behind
Estimate at completion (EAC) See 3.2
Estimate to complete (ETC) EAC − AC (work proceeding as planned), or a bottom-up reestimate
Variance at completion (VAC) BAC − EAC Positive = under planned cost
To-complete performance index (TCPI) (BAC − EV) ÷ (BAC − AC) to meet the BAC; (BAC − EV) ÷ (EAC − AC) to meet the EAC Above 1 harder to complete; 1 same; below 1 easier

3.2 Choose the EAC formula by the assumption

Assumption in the question EAC
Current cost performance will continue (typical variance) BAC ÷ CPI
Future work will go at the planned rate (the variance was a one-off) AC + (BAC − EV)
The original plan is no longer valid AC + bottom-up ETC
Both CPI and SPI affect the remaining work AC + [(BAC − EV) ÷ (CPI × SPI)]

3.3 Worked example

BAC = 500,000; at the status date PV = 240,000, EV = 200,000, AC = 250,000.

Result Calculation
CV 200,000 − 250,000 = −50,000 (over budget)
SV 200,000 − 240,000 = −40,000 (behind)
CPI 200,000 ÷ 250,000 = 0.80 (80 cents of value per dollar)
SPI 200,000 ÷ 240,000 = 0.83
EAC, typical 500,000 ÷ 0.80 = 625,000; ETC = 625,000 − 250,000 = 375,000; VAC = −125,000
EAC, one-off 250,000 + (500,000 − 200,000) = 550,000; VAC = −50,000
EAC, CPI and SPI 250,000 + 300,000 ÷ (0.80 × 0.833) = 700,000; VAC = −200,000
TCPI (BAC) 300,000 ÷ 250,000 = 1.20 (must work 20% more efficiently)
TCPI (EAC 625,000) 300,000 ÷ 375,000 = 0.80
Percent complete, spent, planned EV ÷ BAC = 40%; AC ÷ BAC = 50%; PV ÷ BAC = 48%

If the BAC is no longer viable, forecast with the EAC; once the EAC is approved it may replace the BAC in the TCPI calculation (PMBOK 8). A TCPI far above 1 signals the BAC is probably out of reach Beyond PMBOK 8rule of thumb.

3.4 Earned value measurement and budget build-up

  • Measuring EV: PMBOK 8 mentions weighted milestones, fixed formula and percent complete (the common 0/100 and 50/50 rules are Beyond PMBOK 8); the rules are set in the financial management plan (Topic 17). EV measures work in budget terms, not value to the customer (Topic 10).
  • Budget build-up: work package estimates (+ activity contingency) → cost baseline (includes contingency reserve in the common variant) → + management reserve = total funds. Contingency reserve is part of the baseline; management reserve is not (Topics 17 and 21).

4Risk Calculations (Process Task 6 and Business Environment Task 5)

Formula Meaning
Score = probability × impact Qualitative ranking. PMBOK 8's example matrix (Figure 5-14) uses probabilities 0.10, 0.30, 0.50, 0.70, 0.90 and impacts 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.40, 0.80, so the printed scores run from 0.01 to 0.72 (0.90 × 0.80)
EMV = probability × impact value Threats are negative, opportunities positive (PMBOK 8 glossary: the estimated value of an outcome in monetary terms)
Decision tree: EMV of a branch = sum of (probability × payoff) − cost of the choice; pick the higher EMV PMBOK 8 example: the plant upgrade (decision EMV $46M) beats the new build
Contingency reserve A percentage, a fixed amount or a quantitative-analysis result (PMBOK 8). Summing the EMVs of the threats you will fund is a common estimate Beyond PMBOK 8; a simulation gives a percentile, for example the P80 value minus the base Beyond PMBOK 8
Cost-effective response Respond only if cost < reduction in expected loss (compare with the reduction, not with the whole exposure)

Worked example (EMV).

Risk Probability Impact EMV
Threat A: supplier delay 30% −100,000 −30,000
Threat B: rework 10% −200,000 −20,000
Opportunity C: early-delivery bonus 20% +50,000 +10,000

Net EMV = −40,000; the threats alone = −50,000, so about 50,000 of contingency covers the threats.

Worked example (decision tree). Option X: invest 40,000; 60% chance of +100,000, 40% chance of +20,000: EMV = 60,000 + 8,000 − 40,000 = +28,000. Option Y: invest 20,000; 50% of +70,000, 50% of +10,000: EMV = 35,000 + 5,000 − 20,000 = +20,000. Choose X.

Cost-effectiveness example. A threat has a 25% chance of an 80,000 penalty (EMV −20,000). A 15,000 response cuts the probability to 5% (EMV −4,000). The response removes 16,000 of exposure for 15,000, so it is worth doing.

5Team, Resource and Communication Calculations

Formula Example
Channels = n(n − 1) ÷ 2 Beyond PMBOK 8 6 people: 15 channels; 9 people: 36; a team of 10 has 45, 12 has 66, 20 has 190 (Topic 20)
Capacity = people × available days × focus factor Beyond PMBOK 8 6 × 8 days × 0.7 = 33.6 person-days
Resource utilization = productive hours ÷ available hours Beyond PMBOK 8 30 of 40 hours = 75%
Duration = effort ÷ (people × availability) Section 2.1

PMBOK 8 asks you to consider the number of communication channels when planning; the formula itself is exam practice.

6Value and Financial Calculations (Process Task 6; Topic 10)

PMBOK 8 names these metrics (ROI, IRR, payback period, ROA, ROACE, NPV, cost-benefit analysis, CapEx and OpEx; Table 2-8 uses them to check value) but prints no formulas, so the formulas below are Beyond PMBOK 8.

Measure Formula Decision rule
Present value PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)^n Discount future money to today
NPV Sum of CFt ÷ (1 + r)^t − initial investment (CFt = net cash flow in year t) Accept if NPV > 0; among alternatives choose the higher NPV
IRR The rate at which NPV = 0 Accept if IRR exceeds the required rate; do not rank mutually exclusive projects by IRR alone
Payback period Investment ÷ net annual inflow (even flows); otherwise add cumulative inflows Shorter is better; ignores time value of money and cash after payback
Discounted payback Discount each year's cash flow, then find when the running total turns positive Always later than simple payback; the better test when timing matters
ROI (Benefits − costs) ÷ costs, or net benefit ÷ cost Higher is better: benefits 100,000 against costs 80,000 gives 25%
Benefit-cost ratio (BCR) PV of benefits ÷ PV of costs Above 1 acceptable: 150,000 ÷ 100,000 = 1.5
ROA / ROACE Return on assets (net income ÷ total assets); return on average capital employed Organization-level profitability measures
Opportunity cost The value of the best alternative given up Include it when choosing
Sunk cost Money already spent Ignore it when deciding whether to continue
Break-even Fixed cost ÷ (price − variable cost) Units at which two options cost the same
Depreciation (straight line) (Cost − salvage value) ÷ useful life Spreads an asset's cost over its life

Worked example (diagram). Project A: invest 100,000; inflows 40,000, 50,000 and 60,000 in years 1 to 3; r = 10%. PVs are 36,364, 41,322 and 45,079, so NPV = +22,765; IRR ≈ 21.7%; payback = 2 + 10,000 ÷ 60,000 = 2.17 years; discounted payback: the running discounted total is -63,636, -22,314 and +22,765, so it turns positive after 2 + 22,314 ÷ 45,079 = about 2.5 years. Project B (invest 70,000; inflows 40,000, 40,000 and 20,000) has NPV +14,448, IRR ≈ 22.7% and payback 1.75 years. Choose A: it adds the most value, even though B has the higher IRR and the shorter payback.

Payback and BCR. A 90,000 project with net inflows of 30,000 a year pays back in 90,000 ÷ 30,000 = 3 years; with PV of benefits 120,000 against PV of costs 90,000, BCR = 1.33.

7Procurement Calculations (Process Task 5)

PMBOK 8 (Appendix X4) says make-or-buy analysis may use payback period, ROI, IRR, discounted cash flow, NPV and cost-benefit analysis, and describes target-cost contracts that share savings and overruns; the formulas below are Beyond PMBOK 8.

Topic Formula and example
Make or buy Make = fixed cost + variable cost × units; Buy = price × units; break-even units = fixed cost ÷ (buy price − variable make cost)
Lease or buy Buy 60,000 plus 2,000 a month against lease 5,000 a month: 60,000 + 2,000m = 5,000m, so m = 20 months
Fixed price The price is fixed; the seller keeps savings and bears overruns
Cost-reimbursable Price = actual cost + fee (a fixed fee does not change with cost); the buyer carries cost risk
Time and materials Hours × rate + materials
Fixed price incentive fee Seller fee = target fee + seller share × (target cost − actual cost); price = actual cost + fee, capped at the ceiling price
Point of total assumption (PTA) (Ceiling price − target price) ÷ buyer share + target cost

Worked example. Target cost 200,000, target fee 20,000 (target price 220,000), ceiling 250,000, share 80/20. At an actual cost of 230,000 the seller's fee is 20,000 − 0.2 × 30,000 = 14,000 and the buyer pays 244,000. PTA = (250,000 − 220,000) ÷ 0.8 + 200,000 = 237,500; above it the seller bears every extra dollar (at 260,000 the seller loses 10,000).

Another example. Target cost 100,000, target fee 10,000, ceiling 125,000, share 70/30; actual cost 90,000: fee = 10,000 + 0.3 × 10,000 = 13,000; the buyer pays 103,000.

8Quality and Statistics (Topic 18)

PMBOK 8 describes control charts, control limits and specification limits, and names cost of quality and Six Sigma, but it gives no numeric rules; the figures below are Beyond PMBOK 8 exam practice.

Formula Meaning and example
Bands: ±1σ 68.27%, ±2σ 95.45%, ±3σ 99.73% A process is "in control" when points stay within the control limits
Control limits = mean ± 3σ Mean 50 and σ = 2: limits 44 and 56
Rule of seven Seven consecutive points on one side of the mean signal a non-random pattern (investigate)
Cost of quality = cost of conformance + cost of nonconformance Prevention and appraisal versus internal and external failure
Six Sigma About 3.4 defects per million opportunities
Pareto The vital few causes (about 80/20)
Cp = (USL − LSL) ÷ 6σ Beyond PMBOK 8 USL 56, LSL 44, σ = 2: Cp = 1.0; σ = 1.5: Cp = 1.33
Cpk = the smaller of (USL − mean) ÷ 3σ and (mean − LSL) ÷ 3σ Beyond PMBOK 8 Mean 52, σ = 2: Cpk = 0.67 (off-center)

9Agile Flow and Status Metrics (Topics 04, 16 and 28)

Metric Formula and example
Velocity Story points accepted per iteration; use the average of recent iterations
Forecast Beyond PMBOK 8 Iterations left = remaining points ÷ average velocity: 140 ÷ ((18 + 22 + 20) ÷ 3 = 20) = 7 iterations (14 weeks of two-week iterations)
Burndown / burnup Remaining work against time; burnup also shows scope added
Cycle time From a task starting to its completion (Kanban)
Lead time From a task entering the board or being requested to its delivery
Throughput Items completed per time period
Little's law Beyond PMBOK 8 Average cycle time = work in progress ÷ throughput: 15 items in progress and 5 done a week gives 3 weeks
WSJF Beyond PMBOK 8 Cost of delay ÷ job size (or duration); do the highest first
Net Promoter Score (named in PMBOK 8) % promoters − % detractors Beyond PMBOK 8formula: 50% promoters and 30% detractors give 20
PMBOK 8 Table 2-6 scope metrics Scope definition accuracy = planned items correctly delivered ÷ total planned × 100. Scope creep = unplanned ÷ total deliverables × 100 and requirements stability = unchanged ÷ total requirements × 100 (PMBOK 8 prints these two inverted; Topic 15)

10Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Schedule CPM, float, PERT, SV and SPI Velocity forecast, burnup and burndown, cycle time Milestone dates from CPM; iteration forecasts inside
Cost EVM against the cost baseline, EAC and TCPI Burn rate, cost per iteration, budget in time-boxed tranches; EVM at milestone level if required Both
Risk EMV, simulation, reserves Risks in the backlog; buffer capacity; reserve as capacity Both
Value NPV, IRR, ROI, BCR at business case and gates Value per iteration, cost of delay, usage and outcome metrics Both
Status Variances and indices with thresholds Velocity, throughput, defects, stakeholder feedback Mixed dashboard

11Tailoring, Interactions and Checking Results

  • Tailor which metrics to use to the approach, contract, regulation and audience: a fixed-price government contract may mandate EVM; a small agile team needs only velocity and a burnup chart. Measure only what is relevant (PMBOK 8).
  • Interactions: estimates (Topic 14) feed baselines (Topics 16 and 17); reserves (Topic 21); variances trigger change requests (Topic 29) and reports (Topic 28); procurement terms shape cost risk (Topic 22); financial metrics tie to the business case (Topic 10).
  • Data quality first: forecasts are only as good as the actuals and the baseline; poor data produces false precision. PMBOK 8 notes AI tools can support forecasting, but humans check the inputs and the outputs (Topic 08).
  • Check results (PMBOK 8 Tables 2-6 and 2-8): CV and CPI for the budget; financial targets with vendors; ROI, NPV, IRR and KPIs for value; schedule and scope metrics for delivery.

12Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. Read the assumption before choosing an EAC formula: typical (BAC ÷ CPI), one-off (AC + BAC − EV), invalid plan (AC + bottom-up ETC), both indices (CPI × SPI).
  2. Mind the direction: CPI or SPI above 1 is favorable; CV and SV are EV minus the comparison value (negative = over budget or behind).
  3. TCPI is remaining work over remaining funds, (BAC − EV) ÷ (BAC − AC), or EAC − AC when the EAC is the goal; do not invert it.
  4. EF = ES + D − 1 under the day-1 convention; check which convention the question states.
  5. Total float versus free float: total float delays the end date, free float delays the next activity.
  6. The critical path is the longest path, not the shortest; it can change after compression.
  7. Triangular divides by 3; PERT weights M by 4 and divides by 6; SD = (P − O) ÷ 6.
  8. EMV signs: threats negative, opportunities positive; compare a response's cost with the reduction in exposure.
  9. Contingency reserve is inside the baseline; management reserve is outside it.
  10. Channels grow quadratically: n(n − 1) ÷ 2, not n.
  11. NPV beats IRR and payback for choosing among alternatives; ignore sunk costs; payback ignores time value.
  12. Above the PTA the seller bears 100% of overruns; the ceiling caps the buyer's price.
  13. Velocity is a forecast tool, not a performance target; do not use it to compare teams (Topic 04).
  14. EV measures work done in budget terms, not value delivered; confirm value separately.
  15. Round at the end, and pick the closest option; do not mix percent and decimal forms.

13Exam Q&A

13.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1At a status date, a project has PV 60,000, EV 54,000 and AC 63,000. Which pair of variances is correct?

  • ASV is +3,000 and CV is -9,000: SV taken as actual cost minus planned value
  • BSV is -6,000 and CV is -9,000: behind schedule and over budget
  • CSV is -9,000 and CV is -6,000: the two variances are swapped
  • DSV is +6,000 and CV is +9,000: ahead of schedule and under budget
Show the answer

Answer: B. Both variances are earned value minus the comparison value: SV equals 54,000 minus 60,000, or -6,000, and CV equals 54,000 minus 63,000, or -9,000, so the project is behind schedule and over budget. The other pairs have the wrong signs, swap the two variances or use the wrong formula.

S2BAC is 500,000, PV 320,000, EV 200,000 and AC 250,000, and both cost and schedule performance are expected to affect the remaining work. What is the EAC?

  • A850,000, using AC plus the remaining work divided by CPI times SPI
  • B730,000, using AC plus the remaining work divided by the SPI alone
  • C625,000, using BAC divided by the current cost performance index only
  • D550,000, using AC plus the remaining planned budget at the planned rate
Show the answer

Answer: A. CPI is 0.8 and SPI is 0.625, so their product is 0.5, and EAC equals 250,000 plus 300,000 divided by 0.5, or 850,000. The other figures apply a formula meant for a different assumption: cost performance only, a one-off variance or schedule performance only.

S3BAC is 800,000, EV 300,000 and AC 400,000, and an EAC of 1,000,000 has been approved. What is the TCPI based on the approved EAC?

  • A0.75, because earned value divided by actual cost gives the current efficiency
  • B0.83, because 500,000 of remaining work is to be done for 600,000 of remaining funds
  • C1.25, because 500,000 of remaining work is to be done for 400,000 of remaining budget
  • D1.20, because the remaining funds divided by the remaining work gives the index
Show the answer

Answer: B. With an approved EAC, TCPI equals (BAC minus EV) divided by (EAC minus AC): 500,000 divided by 600,000 is 0.83, so the remaining work can be done a little less efficiently than planned. The 1.25 figure is the BAC-based index, 0.75 is the CPI, and 1.20 inverts the ratio.

S4Task A (2 days) precedes B (4 days) and C (3 days), and both B and C precede D (5 days). Using the day-1 convention, what is the late start of C?

  • ADay 6, because the late start equals the day before D must start
  • BDay 3, because its late finish of day 6 minus its 3 days gives 3, so C is critical
  • CDay 4, because its late finish of day 6 minus 3 days plus 1 gives 4
  • DDay 5, because the late start is taken as the late finish of day 6 minus one day
Show the answer

Answer: C. D starts on day 7, so C's late finish is day 6; with the day-1 convention LS equals LF minus duration plus 1, or 6 minus 3 plus 1, which is day 4. Omitting the plus 1 gives day 3 and wrongly makes C critical, and the other dates confuse the late start with the late finish.

S5An activity has optimistic 8, most likely 14 and pessimistic 32 days. Using the triangular average that PMBOK 8 prints, what is the expected duration?

  • A14 days, because the most likely value is the best estimate of duration
  • B20 days, because the midpoint of 8 and 32 is the expected duration
  • C18 days, because 8 plus 14 plus 32 divided by 3 gives 18
  • D16 days, because 8 plus 4 times 14 plus 32 divided by 6 gives 16
Show the answer

Answer: C. The triangular average is (optimistic plus most likely plus pessimistic) divided by 3, or 54 divided by 3, which is 18 days. The 16-day figure is the PERT beta formula, the most likely value ignores the range, and the midpoint ignores the most likely value.

S6A PERT estimate has an expected duration of 16 days and a standard deviation of 4 days. Between which durations is completion about 68% likely?

  • A16 to 20 days, which is the expected value plus one standard deviation
  • B8 to 24 days, which is the expected value plus or minus two standard deviations
  • C14 to 18 days, which is the expected value plus or minus half a deviation
  • D12 to 20 days, which is the expected value plus or minus one standard deviation
Show the answer

Answer: D. About 68% of outcomes fall within one standard deviation of the mean, so 16 plus or minus 4 gives 12 to 20 days. Two standard deviations cover about 95%, and the other ranges use the wrong width or only one side.

S7Expanding costs 30,000 with a 50% chance of a 100,000 return and a 50% chance of 20,000. Piloting costs 15,000 with a 70% chance of 40,000 and a 30% chance of 10,000. Which is better by EMV?

  • APilot, with an EMV of +31,000 because the investment is not deducted
  • BExpand, with an EMV of +30,000 against +16,000 for the pilot
  • CPilot, with an EMV of +16,000 against +30,000 for expanding
  • DExpand, with an EMV of +60,000 because the investment is not deducted
Show the answer

Answer: B. Expanding has an EMV of 50,000 plus 10,000 minus 30,000, or +30,000, and piloting has 28,000 plus 3,000 minus 15,000, or +16,000, so expanding is better. Ignoring the cost of the choice gives 60,000 and 31,000, and reversing the comparison picks the lower value.

S8A project requires an investment of 50,000 and returns 55,000 after one year. The required rate is 10%. What is the NPV, and what does it mean?

  • ANPV is -5,000, so the project destroys value and should be rejected
  • BNPV is +55,000, so the project returns more than its whole investment
  • CNPV is zero, so the project only earns the required return and is marginal
  • DNPV is +5,000, so the project creates 5,000 of value and should be accepted
Show the answer

Answer: C. The present value of 55,000 received in a year at 10% is 50,000, which equals the investment, so NPV is zero and the project earns exactly the required return. The undiscounted gain of 5,000 ignores the time value of money.

S9Project X has a payback of three years and a benefit-cost ratio of 1.25. Project Y has a payback of two years and a benefit-cost ratio of 0.9. Which statement is supported?

  • ANeither can be judged, because payback and the benefit-cost ratio cannot be compared
  • BY is better, because its shorter payback shows that it is the stronger investment
  • CBoth are acceptable, because any project that eventually returns its cost is sound
  • DX is acceptable, because a ratio above 1 means benefits exceed costs in present value
Show the answer

Answer: D. A benefit-cost ratio above 1 means the present value of benefits exceeds the present value of costs, so X is acceptable and Y, at 0.9, is not. A shorter payback ignores the time value of money and what happens after payback.

S10Three critical activities can be crashed: X (up to 3 days, 1,500 extra per day), Y (up to 2 days, 1,200 per day) and Z (up to 1 day, 1,800 per day). What is the cheapest way to shorten the project by 3 days?

  • ACrash Y two days and X one day, for 3,900 extra
  • BCrash Y two days and Z one day, for 4,200 extra
  • CCrash Y three days, for 3,600 extra
  • DCrash X three days, for 4,500 extra
Show the answer

Answer: A. Crash the cheapest critical activity first, within its limit: Y for 2 days costs 2,400, then X for 1 day costs 1,500, a total of 3,900. Crashing X alone or Y with Z costs more, and Y cannot be crashed by 3 days.

S11Buying equipment costs 90,000 plus 1,500 a month to maintain, while leasing costs 4,500 a month. After how many months does buying become cheaper than leasing?

  • AAfter 20 months, because 90,000 divided by the lease payment of 4,500 gives 20
  • BAfter 60 months, because 90,000 divided by the maintenance cost of 1,500 gives 60
  • CAfter 15 months, because 90,000 divided by the sum of 6,000 gives 15
  • DAfter 30 months, because 90,000 divided by the monthly difference of 3,000 gives 30
Show the answer

Answer: D. Buying and leasing cost the same when 90,000 plus 1,500 per month equals 4,500 per month, so the break-even is 90,000 divided by 3,000, or 30 months, after which buying is cheaper. The other figures divide by the wrong monthly amount.

S12A fixed price incentive fee contract has a target cost of 150,000, a target fee of 15,000 and a 70/30 buyer/seller share. The actual cost is 135,000, below the ceiling. What does the buyer pay?

  • A154,500, which is the actual cost plus a fee of 19,500
  • B150,000, which is the target cost with no fee at all
  • C165,000, which is the target price regardless of the actual cost
  • D135,000, which is the actual cost without any fee
Show the answer

Answer: A. The seller's share of the 15,000 saving is 30%, or 4,500, so the fee is 15,000 plus 4,500, or 19,500, and the price is 135,000 plus 19,500, or 154,500. The target cost, the target price and the cost alone ignore the sharing formula.

13.2 Recall Q&As

R1Give the CV, SV, CPI and SPI formulas.

Show the answer

CV = EV − AC; SV = EV − PV; CPI = EV ÷ AC; SPI = EV ÷ PV.

R2What do CPI and SPI values mean?

Show the answer

Above 1 is favorable (under cost, ahead of schedule), 1 is on plan, below 1 is unfavorable.

R3List the four EAC formulas and when each applies.

Show the answer

BAC ÷ CPI (performance continues); AC + (BAC − EV) (one-off variance); AC + bottom-up ETC (original plan invalid); AC + (BAC − EV) ÷ (CPI × SPI) (both indices matter).

R4How are ETC and VAC calculated?

Show the answer

ETC = EAC − AC (or a bottom-up reestimate); VAC = BAC − EAC.

R5What are the two TCPI formulas and how do you read the result?

Show the answer

(BAC − EV) ÷ (BAC − AC) to meet the BAC; (BAC − EV) ÷ (EAC − AC) to meet the EAC. Above 1 is harder to complete, 1 the same, below 1 easier.

R6What are the CPM day-1 formulas and the float definitions?

Show the answer

EF = ES + D − 1; LS = LF − D + 1. Total float = LS − ES = LF − EF; free float = successor's ES − EF − 1; zero total float marks the critical path.

R7What is the difference between the triangular and PERT estimates?

Show the answer

Triangular = (O + M + P) ÷ 3 (PMBOK 8); PERT = (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6 with SD = (P − O) ÷ 6 (Beyond PMBOK 8).

R8What is EMV and how is it used?

Show the answer

Probability × impact value (threats negative, opportunities positive); in a decision tree add the branch EMVs net of cost and choose the higher result.

R9What is the communication channels formula?

Show the answer

n(n − 1) ÷ 2.

R10What are the decision rules for NPV, IRR and payback?

Show the answer

Accept if NPV > 0 and choose the higher NPV among alternatives; accept if IRR exceeds the required rate; shorter payback is better but ignores time value and later cash.

R11How are ROI and BCR calculated?

Show the answer

ROI = (benefits − costs) ÷ costs; BCR = PV of benefits ÷ PV of costs (above 1 is acceptable).

R12What percentages do ±1, ±2 and ±3 standard deviations cover?

Show the answer

About 68.27%, 95.45% and 99.73%; control limits sit at the mean ± 3σ.

R13What is the point of total assumption?

Show the answer

(Ceiling price − target price) ÷ buyer share + target cost; above it the seller bears all additional cost.

R14How do you forecast an agile finish and relate cycle time to flow?

Show the answer

Iterations left = remaining points ÷ average velocity; cycle time = work in progress ÷ throughput (Little's law); lead time runs from request to delivery, cycle time from start to done.
